## Learning objectives

1. Describe the three parts of a `.qmd` file and what each does.
2. Write prose with Markdown: headings, emphasis, lists, links, tables.
3. Embed R code so that results appear in the output document.
4. Control chunk behaviour with options (`echo`, `eval`, `warning`, `fig-cap`).
5. Render the same source to HTML, Word and Reveal.js slides.

## What a `.qmd` file is

Three ingredients, in this order:

```` markdown
---
title: "Knowledge gain in a flipped classroom"
author: "Dr A. Nair"
format: html
---

## Background                            <-- 2. prose, in Markdown

The flipped classroom has been proposed as...

```{{r}}                                  <-- 3. code, in chunks
library(tidyverse)
students <- read_csv("data/meded_students.csv")
mean(students$gain, na.rm = TRUE)
```
````

1. **YAML header** between `---` fences: metadata and output settings.
2. **Markdown prose**: what you would have written in Word.
3. **Code chunks**: what you would have done in SPSS, except it stays.

Render, and Quarto runs the code and drops the results into the prose. Change
the data, render again, and every number updates. Nothing is copied by hand.

::: {.callout-important}
## This is the whole idea
The alternative (run the analysis, copy the number, paste into Word, format
the table) breaks silently the moment anything changes. And something always
changes: a duplicate is found, an exclusion criterion shifts, a reviewer asks
for a subgroup.
:::

## Markdown in ninety seconds

| You write | You get |
|---|---|
| `## Methods` | A level-2 heading |
| `*italic*`, `**bold**` | *italic*, **bold** |
| `- item` | Bullet list |
| `1. item` | Numbered list |
| `[text](https://url)` | A hyperlink |
| `![caption](figure.png)` | An image |
| `` `code` `` | `inline code` |
| `> quoted` | A block quote |

Tables use pipes:

```markdown
| Arm | n | Mean gain |
|-----|---|-----------|
| Flipped | 120 | 12.4 |
| Traditional | 120 | 7.1 |
```

Blank lines matter. Two lines of text with no blank line between them become
one paragraph.

## Code chunks and their options

Chunk options go at the top of the chunk, after `#|`:

````markdown
```{{r}}
#| label: fig-gain
#| fig-cap: "Knowledge gain by teaching arm."
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
ggplot(students, aes(teaching_arm, gain)) + geom_boxplot()
```
````

The ones you will use constantly:

| Option | Effect | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `echo: false` | Hide the code, show the result | Manuscripts |
| `eval: false` | Show the code, do not run it | Teaching, examples |
| `include: false` | Run it, show nothing | Setup chunks |
| `warning: false`, `message: false` | Suppress noise | Package loading |
| `fig-cap:` | Caption the figure | Always, in papers |
| `label: fig-...` | Make it cross-referenceable | Always, in papers |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Set them once, globally
Put defaults in the YAML rather than repeating them in thirty chunks:

```yaml
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
```
:::

## Inline code: where the magic actually lives

```markdown
The mean knowledge gain was `r knitr::inline_expr("round(mean(students$gain, na.rm = TRUE), 1)")` points.
```

Renders as: *The mean knowledge gain was 9.8 points.*

That number is not typed. It is computed at render time. When you find two
duplicated records next month and re-run, the sentence corrects itself. Every
number in your results section can work this way, and once you have done it
once you will not go back.

## Cross-references

```markdown
As shown in @fig-gain, the flipped arm gained more.
See @tbl-baseline for the cohort characteristics.
```

Label chunks `fig-something` for figures and `tbl-something` for tables, and
Quarto numbers them, links them, and renumbers when you reorder. No more
"Figure 3 (now Figure 4)".

## Citations

Put a `.bib` file next to your document, point the YAML at it, and cite with
`@key`:

```yaml
---
bibliography: references.bib
csl: vancouver.csl
---
```

```markdown
Reproducibility is the minimum standard [@peng2011].
```

Quarto builds the reference list, in the style you name, from only the
citations you actually used. Zotero exports `.bib` directly (Better BibTeX
keeps the keys stable, worth installing).

## One source, many outputs

```yaml
format:
  html:  {toc: true}
  docx:  {reference-doc: template.docx}
  pdf:   {documentclass: article}
  revealjs: {slide-level: 2}
```

Then:

```{r}
#| eval: false
quarto::quarto_render("report.qmd")                    # all formats
quarto::quarto_render("report.qmd", output_format = "docx")
```

Or click **Render** in RStudio, using the dropdown to pick a format.

::: {.callout-note}
## The Word workflow that actually survives co-authors
Render to `docx`. Send it. Co-authors track-change the Word file. You read
their changes and make the corresponding edits **in the `.qmd`**, then
re-render. Yes, that is a manual step, but the source of truth stays
singular. The alternative, editing the Word file directly, forks your project
permanently.
:::

# Hands-on {#hands-on}

**14:45 – 15:15.** Thirty minutes. The goal is one rendered document
containing prose, a table and a figure.

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 1: your first rendered document"}
**Time:** 10 minutes

1. **File → New File → Quarto Document**. Title: "Knowledge gain: first
   look". Format: HTML.
2. Delete everything below the YAML header.
3. Add a `## Background` heading and two sentences about the flipped
   classroom study.
4. Add a setup chunk that loads `tidyverse` and reads
   `data/meded_students.csv`, with `#| include: false`.
5. Save as `report.qmd` in your project root and click **Render**.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution 1" collapse="true"}
````markdown
---
title: "Knowledge gain: first look"
author: "Your name"
date: today
format: html
---

## Background

Three medical colleges compared a flipped classroom against traditional
lectures on a module in evidence-based practice. Students were assessed
before and after with the same knowledge test.

```{{r}}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
students <- read_csv("data/meded_students.csv")
```
````

`include: false` runs the chunk but shows neither code nor output, exactly
what you want for loading packages and data.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 2: add a figure, a table and a live number"}
**Time:** 15 minutes

Extend `report.qmd`:

1. A `## Results` section.
2. A code chunk producing your boxplot of `gain` by `teaching_arm`, with
   `#| label: fig-gain`, a `fig-cap`, and `echo: false`.
3. A small summary table (count and mean gain per arm) printed with
   `knitr::kable()`.
4. One sentence in the prose that reports the overall mean gain using
   **inline code**, not a typed number.
5. Reference the figure in the text with `@fig-gain`.
6. Render.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution 2" collapse="true"}
````markdown
## Results

```{{r}}
#| label: fig-gain
#| fig-cap: "Knowledge gain by teaching arm."
#| echo: false
ggplot(students, aes(x = teaching_arm, y = gain, fill = teaching_arm)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.75) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Gain (post − pre)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

```{{r}}
#| label: tbl-arm
#| tbl-cap: "Knowledge gain by teaching arm."
#| echo: false
students |>
  group_by(teaching_arm) |>
  summarise(
    n         = sum(!is.na(gain)),
    mean_gain = round(mean(gain, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    sd_gain   = round(sd(gain, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Across the cohort, mean knowledge gain was
`r knitr::inline_expr("round(mean(students$gain, na.rm = TRUE), 1)")` points
(@fig-gain). Eleven students without a post-test are excluded from all
gain calculations.
````

The last sentence is the important one: the number is computed, and the
exclusion is stated in the text rather than buried.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 3 (stretch): change the format"}
**Time:** 5 minutes

1. Change `format: html` to `format: docx`. Render. Open the Word file.
2. Now try:

```yaml
format:
  html: default
  docx: default
```

3. Render again. Both appear. Same source, no retyping.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution 3" collapse="true"}
Nothing more to write. That is the point of the exercise. If `docx` fails,
close any open Word document with the same name; Word locks the file and
Quarto cannot overwrite it. This will happen to you at least twice.

For PDF you also need `tinytex::install_tinytex()`, see
[Setup](../prelude/install.qmd).
:::

## Key takeaways

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
- A `.qmd` is YAML + Markdown + code chunks.
- Chunk options control what the reader sees; `echo: false` for manuscripts,
  `include: false` for setup.
- Inline code is how numbers in your prose stay correct.
- Label figures `fig-*` and tables `tbl-*` and let Quarto do the numbering.
- One source, many formats. Never maintain two versions of a document.
:::
